newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper denies links with cocaine kings.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper denies links with cocaine kings.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper said on Thursday he only ever struck one pact with Colombia's notorious Cali drug mob -- to put all its bosses behind bars and shoot those who tried to escape.
Talking to reporters in Bogota, he rejected as "grotesquely false" a series of allegations made this week by Guillermo Pallomari, the former Cali cartel accountant, during a drug trial in Miami.

Pallomari testified that Samper, before his election as president in 1994, dined with cartel kingpins Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela to discuss terms for their surrender. He also reiterated claims that Samper had knowingly received a multi-million dollar campaign donation from the billionaire cocaine barons.
"I did make a deal -- to capture all the members of the Cali cartel ... and I said that those who escaped and resisted re-arrest would be shot. I have fulfilled that," Samper said.

The Rodriguezes were captured in mid-1995 and were sentenced earlier this year to what have been criticised as "ridiculously lenient" prison terms. And the cartel No.3 Jose "Chepe" Santacruz was shot to death in early 1996 after he walked out of a Bogota top-security prison.
"They (the Rodriguezes) in return promised they would try to kill me, but fortunately they have not kept their side of the bargain," he added.

Pallomari is the star prosecution witness in the so-called "Cornerstone" trial of two U.S. lawyers, one of them a former Justice Department official sand four South Florida smugglers on charges of drug trafficking and obstructing justice.
The Chilean-born accountant's testimony has contained many details about Samper's alleged links with the Rodriguezes, once said to be responsible for 80 percent of the world cocaine supply.

In a statement issued early on Thursday, Samper's lawyer, Luis Guillermo Nieto Roa, condemned the Miami court for "mud slinging" at Samper. Despite extensive media coverage within Colombia, the "cornerstone" trial has failed to whip up a political storm like the one that almost toppled Samper when the accusations first surfaced.
"It's obvious this is a frame-up in which the U.S. government is clearly aiming to produce political effects in Colombia," Nieto Roa said in a statement.
Many of the allegations involving Samper were the subject of a Colombian congressional inquiry last year in which the president was cleared of any wrongdoing.
U.S. anti-drug officials have dismissed the findings of Congress, dominated by Samper's ruling Liberal Party, and insist he is "truly corrupt president" with known ties to drug traffickers.
Last week Samper described the Miami trial as "the same movie as before but in English".
